title: Shaking the palace
hook: Moggallana shakes the god Sakka's palace with his toe to wake him from pride

segments.voice: Yesterday: the greater Saccaka, and your line, it didn't invade. When something strong came, pleasant or not, could you feel it without being taken over? Day four hundred thirty-two.

Sakka is king of the gods of the Thirty-Three, one of the heavens in Buddhist cosmology. One day he visits the Buddha and asks a big question in a few words: how is a monk freed by the ending of craving? The Buddha answers briefly. Sakka is delighted, bows, and goes home to heaven. Then the monk Moggallana, sitting nearby, starts to wonder. Did Sakka actually understand that, or did he just enjoy it? Today: shaking the palace.
screen: `SAKKA, KING OF THE GODS, ASKS.` → `A SHORT ANSWER. A HAPPY GOD.` → `DID HE UNDERSTAND IT?`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the shorter discourse on the ending of craving. The heart of the Buddha's answer is one short phrase: nothing is worth clinging to. A monk who has heard that knows everything directly, and whatever feeling comes, pleasant, painful or neither, he sees it as impermanent and lets it go. So Moggallana travels to the heaven of the Thirty-Three to check. He finds Sakka in a garden, surrounded by heavenly music. Moggallana asks about the teaching, and Sakka brushes it aside: we gods are so busy. Instead, he shows off. Come and see my palace, the Vejayanta, built after our victory over the titans. Look at the towers. Look at the rooms. Even the goddesses, shy at the sight of a visiting monk, slip away into their rooms. Moggallana thinks: this god is living too carelessly. So he uses his powers. With his big toe, the text says, he makes the whole palace shake and quake and tremble. Sakka and his court are amazed. Their pride goes quiet. Then Moggallana asks: what did the Buddha tell you, briefly, about the ending of craving? And this time Sakka repeats the teaching back, word for word. He had heard it the first time. He just couldn't hear it from inside the palace. A teaching can delight someone and then slide right past, while they go back to admiring their towers. Sometimes it takes a little shaking.
screen: `NOTHING IS WORTH CLINGING TO` · `MOGGALLANA VISITS THE HEAVEN` · `SAKKA SHOWS OFF HIS PALACE` · `A BIG TOE, AND THE PALACE TREMBLES` · then, large: `SHAKE THE PALACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: shake one assumption. Sit, and think of one thing you're quietly proud of and lean on: a skill, a title, a house, a reputation, being the reasonable one. Picture it as a palace with towers. Now, gently, like a toe tapping the floor, ask: is this worth clinging to? Don't answer quickly. Just feel the walls tremble a little. Then let the picture go and rest with the breath, which needs no palace. The bell holds the time.
Shaking the palace. Moggallana's toe on a god's floor: a little shock that wakes pride enough to hear the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: shake the palace. Today, when you catch yourself showing off, even inwardly, tap the floor lightly with one foot, and remember what's worth clinging to. Day four hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Teachers quote the phrase 'nothing is worth clinging to' from this discourse, and use the story of Moggallana and Sakka to show that even pleasant, heavenly lives can make people careless about practice.

fork.setup: you're Moggallana. you've come to check on a god who heard the Buddha teach, and instead he's giving you a tour of his palace. what do you do?
options: admire the palace politely and leave.
shake the palace, so his pride goes quiet.
fork.reveal: Moggallana shakes the palace with his toe. amazed and humbled, Sakka then repeats the Buddha's teaching back exactly.

original.note: Pali pasada: palace, mansion. Sakka's palace is the Vejayanta pasada.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a monk with superpowers.
what it means: comfort and pride can make us deaf to what we've heard; a little shock can wake us up.
what a scholar hears: in Buddhist cosmology even gods like Sakka are not enlightened by being gods: they are beings in a pleasant birth, still subject to craving and to death.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 37, Culatanhasankhaya Sutta (the shorter discourse on the destruction of craving)

notes: MN 37 paraphrased: Sakka's question, 'nothing is worth adhering to', the heavenly music (five hundred instruments?), Sakka first deflecting the question as too busy, the Vejayanta palace built after victory over the asuras ('titans'), the shy goddesses, the toe, Sakka repeating the teaching. Confirm details.

'Gods of the Thirty-Three' (Tavatimsa) originally described as the heaven 'just above ours'; reviewer changed this to 'one of the heavens in Buddhist cosmology', since Tavatimsa is usually placed second among the sense-sphere heavens, above the Four Great Kings. Confirm the cosmology wording.
'Nothing is worth clinging to' is a paraphrase of the short answer (Bodhi renders it 'nothing is worth adhering to'); sources carry quoted: null.
